passage:
Disha: dinner was a disaster 😔
Mehak: what happened??
Disha: Rajesh Uncle said young people don't know how things were, and went on about the leader. I said the numbers say otherwise. Voices got loud
Mehak: oof. did you win?
Disha: no. then I saw his hands shaking a bit. He said he lost his job in the nineties, so he's scared it'll happen again
Mehak: so that's what's under it
Disha: yeah. I said "I'll get more water, Uncle" and left the table before it got heated. Later I told him I heard him
Mehak: proud of you 🙂
Disha: I'd rather have peace at family dinners than a win 🙂

qa.q: What did Rajesh Uncle say he lost in the nineties?
qa.a: Rajesh Uncle said he lost his job in the nineties.

qa.q: What was Rajesh Uncle worried about, and how did Disha find out?
qa.a: He was afraid that losing his job would happen again; Disha saw his hands shaking and heard him say so.

qa.q: What did Disha do when the voices got loud, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Disha left the table with an excuse to get water before it heated up, keeping the relationship safe, which matters more than winning. 🙂

qa.q: How might Rajesh Uncle have felt about the numbers Disha quoted?
qa.a: Possibly as a young person dismissing what he lived through, which may be why his voice rose.

grounding: Disha clashes with an uncle over politics at dinner, listens for his worry, keeps facts calm and leaves respectfully.

passage:
Friday, late

Big fight at dinner. Mama came from the village and within ten minutes we were arguing about the new factory they want to build near his fields. I said it would bring jobs. He said, "You city boys read one article and think you know everything."

I felt my ears burn. I wanted to win. I had numbers ready from my social science project.

Then Siddharth, my cousin, kicked me under the table. And I looked at Mama properly. His hands were shaking a bit around the glass. He wasn't just arguing. He was scared about his land, about the well water.

So I tried asking. "Mama, what are you most worried will happen?" He talked for a long time about the well his father dug. I told him calmly what I'd read about the pollution rules. When he started shouting again, I said, "Mama, I respect you. Let's finish this tomorrow," and went to wash up.

Later he knocked and gave me a laddoo. We didn't agree. But we're fine.

Madhav

qa.q: Where does the family want to build the new factory?
qa.a: They want to build it near Mama's fields.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when Mama called him a city boy?
qa.a: Madhav felt angry and embarrassed, with burning ears, and wanted to win the argument.

qa.q: What did Madhav do when the talk turned heated, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Madhav said he respected Mama and suggested finishing tomorrow, then left the table, which kept the relationship safe instead of trying to win.

qa.q: What is Mama worried about, underneath the argument?
qa.a: Mama is afraid for his land and the well water his father dug, so the argument is about fear, not only politics.

grounding: It shows a teen clashing with his uncle over politics at dinner, listening for the uncle's worry, staying calm and leaving respectfully when it heats up.

passage:
Saurabh: i messed up at dinner
Suraj: chacha?
Saurabh: ya. election stuff again. he said young people are all brainwashed
Saurabh: i said at least we're not stuck in 1990
Suraj: oof
Saurabh: he went red. chachi said "enough." i got up and said sorry, i'm going to my room
Suraj: honestly that part was good. better than screaming
Saurabh: i was SO angry. he wasn't even listening
Suraj: was he maybe scared about something?
Saurabh: idk. he kept saying "who will protect small shops"
Suraj: his shop's been doing badly na
Saurabh: ...ya. papa said sales are down this year
Suraj: so maybe it's not about ur party. it's about his shop
Saurabh: ok that makes me feel kind of bad
Suraj: say sorry for the 1990 line tmrw. u can still disagree 🙂
Saurabh: ya. i will. not trying to win anymore, just want him to not be mad at me

qa.q: What did Saurabh say to Chacha that made him go red?
qa.a: Saurabh said, "at least we're not stuck in 1990."

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling during the argument?
qa.a: Saurabh felt very angry and unheard, feeling that Chacha was not listening at all.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that was good, and what could he do next?
qa.a: Leaving the table with a sorry when it got heated was good; next he could apologise for the 1990 line and listen for Chacha's worry.

qa.q: What might Chacha be worried about, according to Suraj?
qa.a: Suraj thinks Chacha is worried about his own shop doing badly, which is why he kept asking who will protect small shops.

grounding: It shows a teen who clashes with his uncle over politics at dinner, leaves respectfully when it heats up, and comes to see the uncle's worry beneath the argument.
